questions.question:
You want to invest your total amount of R100 ($W = 100$) for buying a number of items from a set. The item $i$ costs $w_i$ rand but gives you a profit of $v_i$. Formulate the Knapsack Problem mathematically using the following data:
$$(v_i, w_i) = \{(7, 20), (5, 30), (8, 15), (4, 10), (3, 30), (9, 25)\}$$
for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, 6$.
questions.modelAnswer:
Decision variables: $x_i = 1$ if item $i$ is chosen, 0 otherwise ($i = 1, \dots, 6$).
Total profit $\sum_{i=1}^{6} v_ix_i$; total money spent $\sum_{i=1}^{6} w_ix_i$.
$$\max\ 7x_1 + 5x_2 + 8x_3 + 4x_4 + 3x_5 + 9x_6$$
$$\text{s.t.}\quad 20x_1 + 30x_2 + 15x_3 + 10x_4 + 30x_5 + 25x_6 \le 100, \qquad x_i \in \{0, 1\}.$$

rubric.point: Budget constraint $\sum w_ix_i \le 100$ with the data

questions.explanation: Follows the lecturer's handwritten solution in Tut2&3.pdf p. 8. Course notes: DisCopt.pdf PDF p. 19 (eqs. 26–29). Knapsack is outside the 2026 exam scope (topic 12).

questions.question:
You want to invest your total amount of R100 ($W = 100$) for buying a number of items from a set. The item $i$ costs $w_i$ rand but gives you a profit of $v_i$. Formulate the Knapsack Problem mathematically using the following data:
$$(v_i, w_i) = \{(7, 20), (5, 30), (8, 15), (4, 10), (3, 30), (9, 25)\}$$
for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, 6$.
Solve (manually) the problem you have formulated in question 1 using the local improvement algorithm starting from $x^0 = (101010)$.
Hints:
(a) Construct the Penalty Function
$$F(x; R) = f(x) - R\phi(x) \text{ with } R = 20$$
(b) Each pass has a number of epoch and whenever an overall best solution is found (within an epoch), the next epoch starts.
questions.solution:
Penalty function (maximisation): $F(x; R) = \sum_i v_ix_i - 20\max\{0, \sum_i w_ix_i - 100\}$, $x \in \{0,1\}^6$.
Rules: each epoch flips every unlocked bit of the current point one at a time and evaluates $F$; the best flip is kept and its bit locked. As soon as a flip beats the overall best, that point becomes the new overall best and a new pass starts from it (hint b). A pass that locks every bit without beating the overall best ends the search.
Start: $x^0 = (101010)$: $F = 7 + 8 + 3 = 18$ (cost 65).
Pass 1, epoch 1: $(001010)$: 11; $(111010)$: $7 + 5 + 8 + 3 = 23 > 18$ (cost 95) → new overall best.
Pass 2 from $(111010)$, 23. Epoch 1: $(011010)$: 16, $(101010)$: 18, $(110010)$: 15, $(111110)$: $27 - 20 \cdot 5 = -73$, $(111000)$: 20, $(111011)$: $32 - 20 \cdot 20 = -368$. Best is $(101010)$, 18: lock bit 2. Epoch 2: $(001010)$: 11, $(100010)$: 10, $(101110)$: 22, $(101000)$: 15, $(101011)$: $7 + 8 + 3 + 9 = 27 > 23$ (cost 90) → new overall best.
Pass 3 from $(101011)$, 27. Epoch 1: $(001011)$: 20, $(111011)$: −368, $(100011)$: 19, $(101111)$: $7 + 8 + 4 + 3 + 9 = 31 > 27$ (cost 100) → new overall best.
Pass 4 from $(101111)$, 31. Epoch 1: $(001111)$: 24, $(111111)$: $36 - 20 \cdot 30 = -564$, $(100111)$: 23, $(101011)$: 27, $(101101)$: 28, $(101110)$: 22. Best $(101101)$, 28: lock bit 5. Epoch 2: $(001101)$: 21, $(111101)$: $7 + 5 + 8 + 4 + 9 = 33 > 31$ (cost 100) → new overall best.
Pass 5 from $(111101)$, 33. Epoch 1: best flip $(111001)$, 29 (others 26, 28, 25, −564, 24): lock bit 4. Epoch 2: best $(101001)$, 24: lock bit 2. Epoch 3: best $(101011)$, 27: lock bit 5. Epoch 4: best $(001011)$, 20: lock bit 1. Epoch 5: best $(000011)$, 12: lock bit 3. Epoch 6: $(000010)$, 3. All bits locked and nothing beat 33, so the search stops.
$$x^* = (111101), \qquad F(x^*; R) = f(x^*) = 33,$$
with cost $20 + 30 + 15 + 10 + 25 = 100 \le 100$ (feasible, no penalty). Checking all 64 binary vectors confirms 33 is the true optimum.
